missing_spec_content.spec_text: Ee = 1/2 k e^2 (assuming the limit of proportionality has not been exceeded)
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson presents Ee = ½ke² with no condition attached. It never says the equation only applies if the limit of proportionality has not been exceeded. keyPoints[3].content also extends it to 'a rubber band, or anything elastic' without this condition.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Required practical activity 1: investigation to determine the specific heat capacity of one or more materials. The investigation will involve linking the decrease of one energy store (or work done) to the increase in temperature and subsequent increase in thermal energy stored.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson does not describe the required practical at all. It does not cover the method, linking the energy supplied (work done) to the temperature rise, or how c is found from the results.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: The amount of energy stored in or released from a system as its temperature changes can be calculated using the equation
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson only talks about energy 'needed to warm up' or 'to heat something up' (keyPoints[4].content). It never says that the same equation gives the energy released when a system cools.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be able to recall and apply this equation. ... Students should be able to apply this equation which is given on the Physics equation sheet.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson never tells the student which equations must be memorised and which are given on the equation sheet. Ek = ½mv² and Ep = mgh must be recalled. Ee = ½ke² and ΔE = mcΔθ are given on the sheet.

factual_errors.text: It is 9.8 N/kg on Earth. Use 10 in non-calculator questions unless told otherwise
factual_errors.correction: The specification states that in any calculation the value of g will be given. The student should use the value the question provides. There is no 'non-calculator' rule for choosing g.

factual_errors.text: g = 9.8 N/kg is the standard value. Only use g = 10 N/kg when the question says 'non-calculator' or tells you to use 10.
